hints: formatter changing program behavior
does bract fmt preserve semantics
canonical formatter altering operator precedence or grouping
round-tripping fmt output through the parser
req-0fa6.statement: `bract fmt` only ever changes whitespace, indentation, and brace placement — it must never reorder, re-associate, or drop AST nodes. Formatting a file and reparsing the result must yield the identical AST to parsing the original.

hints: why does bract run print nothing for an expression statement
extra output appearing on stdout from bract run
does bract run print the result like the REPL does
should errors go to stdout or stderr
testing that a program produces no output
req-15e8.statement: `bract run FILE` must produce no implicit output: a program that writes nothing prints nothing, and top-level expression statement results are never auto-printed to stdout (unlike the REPL, which does print results). All error output goes to stderr only, never stdout, on both success and failure paths.

hints: debug print statement left in the lexer
global variable holding variable bindings
state leaking between test runs or REPL invocations
where should output be written from the interpreter
req-1808.statement: No `print()`/`sys.stdout.write`/`sys.stderr.write` outside the CLI entry module — lexer, parser, and evaluator modules communicate exclusively through return values and raised exceptions. Also, no module-level mutable interpreter state (no global dict/list holding variable bindings, call stack, or output); all interpreter state is threaded explicitly through function arguments/return values or an explicit Interpreter/Environment instance.

hints: naming convention for token types
should token type constants be lowercase or an enum
adding a new token type to the lexer
req-18f3.statement: Token type names use SCREAMING_CASE string constants (`LET`, `IDENT`, `INT`, `TILDE`, `NOTEQ`, ...), not enums or lowercase strings.

hints: leaving a TODO in code marked done
stub implementation reported as complete

req-1a35.statement: No TODO/FIXME/`pass`-stub may remain in any module reachable from `bract/__main__.py` once a task claims that module's feature is complete.

hints: REPL prints True instead of true
boolean result formatting in the REPL
why does the REPL output capitalized True/False
printing an evaluated bract value to stdout
does the REPL use Python's repr or bract's own literal spelling for results
req-3103.statement: When the REPL prints an expression result, boolean values must be rendered using bract's own lowercase literal spelling (`true`/`false`), not Python's capitalized `bool` repr (`True`/`False`).

hints: can I use a pip package for this
adding a dependency to bract

requirements.txt for bract
req-45a4.statement: Bract's implementation must use the Python standard library only — never import, pip-install, or list a third-party dependency in any module or dependency file.

hints: where should a new module live in bract
organizing bract into subpackages
adding a second entry point script
should the formatter be its own package
req-5bba.statement: All interpreter modules live directly under `bract/` (e.g. `bract/lexer.py`) — no nested subpackages like `bract/core/parser/`. All three CLI behaviors (bare REPL, `run FILE`, `fmt FILE`) are dispatched from the single `bract/__main__.py`; there is no second top-level script.

hints: adding float support to bract
implicit type coercion between int and string
does bract have floating point numbers
silently converting types in an operator
req-7f41.statement: Bract has exactly three value types — Integer, String, Boolean — plus nil. There is no float type, and no implicit conversion between types anywhere in the language; every operator's operand types are fixed, and a mismatch is always a runtime type error, never a coercion.

hints: tests failing after a change
should I edit the test file to make it pass
test asserts a value that doesn't match my implementation
adjusting an assertion instead of fixing the bug
req-836e.statement: When the test suite is failing, fix the implementation to make tests pass — never modify the test files themselves to make a failing test pass.

hints: if (0) not working as expected
using a string or nil as a condition
condition must be a boolean error
does bract have truthy falsy values
req-938b.statement: if/while conditions must evaluate to a Boolean; there is no truthy/falsy coercion. Values like 0, "", or nil used as a condition are a runtime type error ('line N: condition must be a boolean'), not automatically false.

hints: implementing != in bract
adding a not-equals operator
lexer errors on ! character
how to write not equal in bract
should I special-case != at the parser
req-afaa.statement: There is no `!` token and no `!=` operator anywhere in Bract's grammar — a `!` character is a lex error ('line N: unexpected character '!''), and the parser must not special-case `!=` since it can never reach it. Not-equals is spelled `<>`, at the same precedence as `==`.

hints: what should the REPL prompt text look like
REPL raises an exception on Ctrl-D instead of exiting
EOF handling in the bract REPL
does the REPL print a prompt before reading input
REPL exit code when stdin closes
req-b08f.statement: The interactive REPL's prompt string is exactly `bract> ` (with a trailing space), and EOF on stdin (Ctrl-D) must end the REPL session cleanly with exit code 0 — never raise an uncaught exception.

hints: does false and f() still call f()
short circuit evaluation for and or
side effects in boolean operators not happening
implementing and/or in the evaluator
req-b21c.statement: `and`/`or` always evaluate both operands, left-to-right, regardless of the left operand's value — they never short-circuit. Any side effect of evaluating the right operand always happens. Both operands must be Boolean or it's a runtime error ('line N: operand of 'and'/'or' must be a boolean').

hints: negative number division or modulo rounding
python floor division vs bract's / and %
which way does % round for negative operands
division by zero error
req-bdc2.statement: Integer `/` and `%` rounding direction for operands of differing sign is intentionally left unpinned by the spec — an implementation only needs `(a/b)*b + (a%b) == a` to hold internally and be self-consistent; don't assume Python's own floor-division/modulo sign convention is mandated. Division or remainder by zero is always a runtime error ('line N: division by zero').

hints: should the repl exit on a runtime error
repl error handling behavior
does an error in the repl kill the session
req-c2d2.statement: The REPL does not exit on error — errors are printed and the session continues accepting further input.

hints: DESIGN.md seems wrong or ambiguous
should I edit the spec file to fix an inconsistency
task description contradicts DESIGN.md
updating the frozen language spec
DESIGN.md and the task prompt disagree
req-c6d8.statement: DESIGN.md is frozen (tagged seed-v1) and must never be edited to fix a spec ambiguity, gap, or bug. Corrections only ever arrive as task-prompt text for a specific task; if a task description conflicts with DESIGN.md, treat it as a bug to flag rather than license to guess or to silently patch the spec.

hints: adding array or string indexing with brackets
s[0] syntax support in the parser
convenience bracket notation for strings
does bract support subscript syntax
req-ccbd.statement: There is no subscript/index syntax (`s[0]`) anywhere in Bract's grammar. String indexing exists exclusively through the `at`/`sub` builtins — don't add bracket-indexing parsing as a convenience, even though `call` supports chained calls like `f()()`.

hints: negative number division rounding direction
does bract division floor or truncate
python // gives the wrong answer for negative operands
implementing division and modulo in the evaluator
arithmetic for loop counters going negative
which way does % round for negative operands
req-d083.statement: Integer `/` and `%` truncate toward zero for operands of differing sign: `(a/b)*b + (a%b) == a` holds, and the quotient's magnitude is `floor(|a|/|b|)` with the sign of the mathematical result truncated (not floored) toward zero. Do not implement with Python's `/` or `//` directly, since neither truncates toward zero for mixed-sign operands. Division or remainder by zero is still always a runtime error ('line N: division by zero').

hints: RecursionError when evaluating deeply nested Bract program
deep call chain crashes the interpreter
should function call evaluation recurse through Python
implementing fn calls or block evaluation in the evaluator
hundreds of nested calls or blocks failing
req-d6a8.statement: The evaluator must be iterative with respect to Bract call depth and block nesting: it must not use Python's own call stack (i.e. Python-level recursion) to evaluate nested Bract function calls or nested blocks, since a deeply-recursive or deeply-nested Bract program must not blow the Python recursion limit. Use an explicit stack/work-list for call and block evaluation instead of letting user-controlled nesting depth become Python stack depth.

hints: shortcut interpreter using python eval or exec
compiling bract expressions to python code
using compile() to evaluate an expression
req-da85.statement: The interpreter must be a genuine tree-walker over its own AST — never use Python's `eval`, `exec`, or `compile` to implement Bract execution.

hints: bare assignment x = expr without let or set
reassigning a variable captured by a closure
counter closure isn't updating state
x'' is already declared error
x'' is not declared error
shadowing a variable in an inner scope
req-db6c.statement: `let x = expr;` declares a new binding and errors if `x` is already declared in the same scope ('line N: 'x' is already declared'); `set x = expr;` reassigns an existing binding by walking the scope chain outward and errors if none exists ('line N: 'x' is not declared'). There is no bare `x = expr;` assignment form — that's a parse error.

hints: should a < b < c parse
supporting chained comparisons like python
comparisons do not chain error
parenthesizing comparisons inside and/or
req-e931.statement: The `comparison` grammar rule accepts at most one comp-op. `a < b < c` must be a parse error ('line N: comparisons do not chain'), not parsed as `a < b and b < c`. Writing the chained meaning requires explicit parens: `(a < b) and (b < c)` — `a < b and b < c` without parens is fine only because each `and` operand independently has zero-or-one comp-op.

hints: is bract fmt idempotent
running fmt twice produces different output
formatter output stability
does formatting an already-formatted file change it again
what test should the formatter's own test file include
req-e991.statement: `bract fmt` output must be byte-stable: running the formatter on its own output must be a no-op (fmt∘fmt = fmt).

hints: python traceback leaking to the user
uncaught exception in bract run
what exit code for a runtime error
formatting error messages consistently across lexer/parser/interpreter
req-f95a.statement: Every lex/parse/runtime error is rendered as exactly one `line N: <message>` line on stderr, produced through one shared error-formatting path — never a Python traceback, exception class name, ANSI color, or extra lines. Exit codes are exactly {0: success, 1: runtime error, 2: lex/parse error}, produced only by `bract run` and top-level CLI dispatch.

hints: concatenating strings with plus
TypeError adding a string and an int
how do I join two strings in bract
+'' cannot be applied to strings
req-fac5.statement: `~` is the only string concatenation operator, and only valid on two strings ('line N: '~' expects strings' otherwise). `+` is exclusively integer addition — applying it to any string operand is a type error ('line N: '+' cannot be applied to strings'), never silent coercion or concatenation.

hints: off-by-one in string indexing
at(s,0) behavior
is sub inclusive or exclusive at the end
porting python slicing semantics to bract
index out of range for string builtin
req-fc94.statement: String builtins (`len`, `at`, `sub`) are 1-indexed, not 0-indexed. `at(s,1)` is the first character; `at(s,0)` is out of range (not the last character, not the first). `sub(s,start,end)` is inclusive on both ends — unlike Python's `s[start:end]`, which is exclusive at the end.
